# Why is textarea filled with mysterious white spaces?

You are encountering a classic rendering quirk where the visible content area of your input field does not align with the logical start of the text cursor. In your specific case, the PHP logic `if($siteLink_val) echo $siteLink_val;` successfully injects data into the DOM, yet the browser renders that data with an invisible offset. When you tab into the field, the caret appears suspended in the middle rather than at the beginning of the string.

This behavior is almost universally caused by a mismatch between the `cols` attribute and the CSS `width` property, combined with how browsers calculate intrinsic width versus explicit styling. The HTML standard dictates that the `cols` attribute defines the number of character columns the textarea should occupy. Historically, before CSS became dominant, this was the primary way to size inputs. However, modern rendering engines prioritize the CSS `width` property when calculating the layout box.

When you apply `style="width:350px;"` alongside `cols="42"`, you create a conflict. The browser calculates the intrinsic width based on the font metrics of "42 columns," but then applies your explicit 350px constraint. If the calculated intrinsic width (based on the default or current font size) is larger than 350px, the browser truncates the visual box. Crucially, however, the internal scrollable areaâthe logical coordinate system where text is storedâoften remains tied to the `cols` definition in legacy rendering logic.

This discrepancy manifests as an invisible padding on the left side of the textarea. The text "sits" further to the right because the browser has shrunk the container visually but failed to shift the internal content origin accordingly. The result is that your PHP echo output, which occupies the full logical width defined by `cols`, appears indented relative to the new, narrower visual edge created by the CSS.

To resolve this, you must align the explicit CSS with the implicit HTML attributes or remove one of them entirely. The most robust approach for modern development is to rely solely on the CSS `width` and `height` properties, removing the deprecated `cols` and `rows` attributes unless you are working in a legacy environment that strictly requires them.

Here is how you should refactor the element:

```html
<textarea 
    name="sitelink" 
    style="width: 350px; height: 80px;"
>
<?php if($siteLink_val) echo $siteLink_val; ?>
</textarea>
```

By removing `cols="42"` and `rows="5"`, you eliminate the source of the coordinate mismatch. The browser will now calculate the internal scrollable area strictly based on the 350px width and the font metrics within that box. If the text is too long, a scrollbar will appear naturally without introducing an offset cursor position.

If you must retain the `cols` attributeâfor instance, to enforce specific character limits in older applicationsâyou must ensure the CSS `width` matches the intrinsic width of that column count exactly. You can approximate this by calculating `width: Xch;` where X is your column count, though this is less reliable across different user font settings than using a pixel-based width with matching content logic.

Another potential pitfall involves the font-family and font-size used in the stylesheet. If you define a global font size for inputs but then set a specific `width: 350px` without accounting for padding, the effective area for text decreases further, exacerbating the offset issue. Always check your CSS reset or base styles to ensure no unexpected padding is being added via `box-sizing`.

In scenarios where you are building forms with Laravel, this alignment issue can also stem from how Blade templates merge inline styles with global CSS classes. Ensure that any helper methods generating the textarea field do not inadvertently add conflicting attributes. If you are using a package like `laravel-company` for specific form handling, verify their documentation to see if they offer standardized components that abstract away these low-level attribute conflicts.

Ultimately, the cleanest solution is to treat the textarea as a purely CSS-driven component. Let the browser handle the aspect ratio and internal scrolling logic based on the explicit pixel dimensions you provide, rather than fighting against legacy character-column calculations. This ensures the cursor always appears exactly where the user expects it: at the very beginning of the input buffer.
